title: Studyflows
aliases:

---

Studyflows are BPMN-based diagrams to describe research workflows. They can be used to visually describe the study protocol, data collection, analysis pipeline, or any other steps in a study. Studyflows facilitate communication with participants (e.g., by automatically running a study), researchers (e.g., by reproducible protocols and analyses), systems (e.g., by automated data processing), and other stakeholders.

Here is an example of a simple studyflow:


![A visual representation of a simple studyflow that describes an experiment (click on the image to enlarge).](../assets/bpmn/studyflow_example_01.png){width="80%" .lightbox}


Although studyflows are visual, the underlying storage format is machine-readable. This allows for automated execution, validation, versioning, and simulation of studyflows. Studyflows can be created using diagramming tools such as [Studyflow Modeler](https://behaverse.org/studyflow-modeler).

The machine-readable structure of a studyflow is defined by the [studyflow schema](https://behaverse.org/schemas/studyflow) in [`behaverse/schemas`](https://github.com/behaverse/schemas); its elements and fields are documented in the [Studyflow schema reference](/spec/studyflow/index.qmd).

## The two kinds of "studyflow" files in a dataset

It is important to note that a dataset may contain two kinds of "studyflow" files: a single study-level studyflow file and agent-level studyflow files.

The study-level studyflow file is the BPMN-based, human- and machine-readable file that covers a study's full lifecycle, including its design, execution, data collection, data processing, and reporting. This file is called `studyflow.xml` and lives at the root of the dataset. This study-level studyflow file is typically not available in open datasets and needs to be reconstructed with information from different sources (e.g., publication, supplementary materials).

For more information on studyflows, see the [Studyflow Modeler](https://behaverse.org/studyflow-modeler) (i.e., the visual editor for studyflow diagrams) and the [Studyflow Specification](https://behaverse.org/studyflow-modeler/docs/) for the complete list of supported elements and their attributes.

The agent-level studyflow file is called `studyflow_log.csv`. It describes in tabular format the timestamped sequence of activities a specific agent engaged with in the context of a study. There is one such file per agent, at the root of that agent's folder (e.g., `data/agent_001/studyflow_log.csv`), because each agent may traverse the design differently (e.g., they may be assigned to different activities, they may drop out or restart activities).

Together both types of files make an agent's path auditable: the design states (among other things) what was possible, and the per-agent record states which of it occurred.

## The run log (`studyflow_log.csv`)

`studyflow_log.csv` is the **run log**: one row per *activity run*, where a run is a single execution of one activity by one agent. Restarting an activity produces another run, and therefore another row. It is defined by the `StudyflowLog` table of the trial schema—see the [field-by-field reference](/spec/trial/studyflow-log.qmd). The pair of names states the pairing plainly: `studyflow.xml` defines the study—the process agents move through—and `studyflow_log.csv` records what happened to a particular agent as they did.

Each row records:

- **which run it was**—`runtime_id`, the identifier every other table uses to refer back to this run, together with `attempt`, `instrument_repetition`, and `timeline_repetition`;
- **where it sits in the study**—`agent_id`, `session_index`, `session_uuid`, `activity_index`, `instrument_id`, and `timeline_id`;
- **how it went**—`status` and, where relevant, `abandon_reason`;
- **when it happened**—`start_datetime`, `end_datetime`, and `anchor_datetime`, the point that ties the run's monotonic clock to wall-clock time.

Because a run that was started and abandoned before producing any data still gets a row, the run log is what makes incomplete participation visible. A dataset's data files show only the runs that produced data; `studyflow_log.csv` shows every run that was begun, which is what tells a reader whether a missing activity was skipped, abandoned, or never assigned.

`runtime_id` is also what makes local identifiers unambiguous. Identifiers such as `response_id` are unique only *within* a run, so the dataset-wide key for a row is the pair `(runtime_id, response_id)`.
